units: the inner circulation of the tree starts up again at the end of the cold season
the feeding liquid climbs from the root system towards the top of the tree
the pressure gap between waterlogged ground and dry air drives that rise
a very thin living tissue under the protective layer of the trunk carries this liquid
the growth organs open and let out a folded blade
through the warm season the foliage makes reserves of sugar
the tree stores those reserves in the trunk and in the roots
in the leaf-fall season the foliage loses its green colouring
through the cold season the tree keeps a faint breathing
the cycle repeats only if the base of the trunk stays sound and water keeps coming
text: As soon as the cold loosens its grip, a tree sets about a piece of work that nobody can watch. Sap climbs from the roots to the highest branches, driven by the gap in pressure between sodden ground and air that is still dry. A thin sleeve of living cells, tucked under the bark, carries that sweet flow upward. Buds swell, split, and let out a leaf folded like a fan. Through the warm months those leaves build sugars, and the tree banks them away in its trunk and in its roots. When the turn comes, the green pigment drains out of the foliage and the leaves let go. Winter looks like sleep, yet the tree breathes faintly and lives off what it has put by. The whole round begins again, year upon year, so long as the base of the trunk stays sound and the roots reach water deep down.

units: someone the narrator knows told of an incident in his hedge
he had seen a round opening dug under a shrub
he shut that opening with a slab of stone to see off a small mammal
the leaves of the shrub yellowed a fortnight after the blocking
the underground tunnel was in fact carrying away the rain
the blocking turned the foot of the bed into a hollow where water stood
the roots left without air died back
he lifted the slab away and cut a drainage channel
the shrub recovered its strength the following season
text: A fellow I know told me what happened in his hedge, and it is worth hearing. He had spotted a neat round hole under one of the shrubs, a burrow by the look of it, and he dropped a flat stone over the mouth to see off whatever small creature had moved in. A fortnight later the leaves on that shrub went a dull yellow and curled at the edges. When he dug the ground open, he saw at once what he had done to it. The tunnel had been doing the work of a drain, carrying off the rain that gathered under the hedge. Block it, and the foot of the bed becomes a basin. Water stood there, the roots had no air left to them, and they died back. He lifted the stone away, cut a channel out towards the ditch, and by the next season the shrub had come back strong. He looks at holes rather differently now.

units: a sharp cold snap at the end of the cold season can destroy an orchard crop in one night
ice crystals damage the open blossom and the recent shoots
watching the sky in the evening is advised to judge the danger
no cloud and no wind mean a high risk
watering the ground moderately before the temperature falls helps hold the warmth
wrapping the weakest trunks in a breathable cloth without tightening it is recommended
no cutting at all should be done on the branches at this time
every cut leaves a wound that the cold makes worse
at sunrise the frosted branches should be sprayed with lukewarm water little by little
writing the episode down is advised to keep a memory of the seasons
text: A late frost can wipe out an orchard crop in a single night: ice burns the open blossom and the tender young shoots. Here is how to keep the losses down. Look up at the sky late in the evening, for a clear sky with no wind is the warning. Then water the ground lightly before the temperature falls, since damp earth takes up warmth and hands it back through the night. Wrap the frailest trunks in a breathable cloth, loosely, so that air still moves around them. Cut nothing at all at this stage, however untidy the growth looks, because every cut leaves a wound and the cold makes short work of a wound. At sunrise, spray the frosted branches with lukewarm water, slowly, a little at a time. Then write the night down in a notebook. Seasons remembered will guide you better than any gadget.

units: one side of the valley is covered with dense woodland growth
there is a bed of rotting plant matter and a smell of living soil
the opposite side still carries the marks of felling done long ago
on that bare side the rock shows and water cuts grooves in it
the thin grass cover there does not hold the feeding layer of soil
a worker in charge of the area walks visitors from one side to the other
she explains that under the trees water sinks in instead of running off the surface
the water point at the foot of the valley is still flowing late in the warm season
gradual planting has begun on the stripped slope with species that root wide and shallow
the outcome will not be visible for several decades
text: On the slope that faces the sunrise the wood has taken hold again: crowded trunks, a deep bed of rotting leaves, a smell of damp earth that clings to the fingers. The far slope still carries the memory of old felling. Bare rock breaks the surface, rain scores it with runnels, and cropped grass can barely hold the fertile skin of soil in place. The warden walks visitors from one flank to the other, so that the contrast stops being an argument and becomes a thing you stand in. Under the canopy, she says, rain soaks in rather than races off, and the spring at the foot of the valley is still running when the heat has worn on. Opposite, the same shower tears downhill and hands the stream a load of red silt. Replanting has begun, shrub by shrub, with species rooted wide and shallow. The change will show in a generation, not before.

units: the outermost layer is thin and waxy and limits the loss of water
the middle layer holds salts of lime and provides the strength
the inner layer is suppler and gives the muscles their anchorage
plates set across the back keep the organs out of harm
the jointed rings of the rear part allow the body to fold
the joints of the limbs bend in one direction only
sensing bristles lodged in fine pores pick up movement in the water
this casing has the drawback of being unable to grow larger
the animal must leave its casing at intervals and wait for the fresh one to harden
through that soft spell it hides under a stone
text: The shell of a crustacean reads like armour built up plate by plate. Its outer skin is thin and waxy; it sheds water and slows the drying of the body. Beneath that lies a stiff layer, loaded with salts of lime, and this is what gives the whole thing its hardness. A third layer, suppler than the rest, lines the inside and gives the muscles something to pull against. Plates across the back keep the organs out of harm. The ringed segments of the tail let the body curl. The legs meet at hinges that bend one way and no other. Fine bristles, lodged in tiny pores, pass on every tremor in the water. All that armour carries one flaw: it will not stretch. Every so often the animal must split it, back out of it, and wait while the fresh casing hardens. Through those soft days it lies low under a pebble.

units: the author finds the lack of response to the retreat of pollinating insects unacceptable
the first warnings lay in field observations ignored some thirty years ago
successive counts then established a steady fall in numbers
fruit growers noticed that the fertilising grains were spreading badly
orchards had to fall back on artificial fertilising that is costly and unreliable
the author holds that the burden of proof should change sides
he claims that damaging practice should prove it does no harm
strips of flowers along the field edge are named as a cheap remedy
keeping the hedges and mowing less often are among the answers put forward
text: Nothing excuses the calm with which we watch the pollinating insects go. The first signals were set down a generation ago, in field notes that nobody thought worth reading twice. Then came the repeated counts, and they showed numbers falling season after season, steadily and without argument. Growers of fruit found next that pollen was moving badly, and that orchards now wanted pollination by hand, an expensive business and a fragile one. We have reached the point where the burden of proof ought to change hands: it is no longer for naturalists to demonstrate the peril, but for damaging practice to demonstrate its innocence. A strip of flowers along a field, a hedge left standing, a mower run less often, and the harm begins to mend for very little. Doing nothing is what will be paid for, and paid for long.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman heading an establishment that raises young trees had not intended this trade
she was studying the chemical make-up of soils
a disease striking the young plants of her district changed her course
the seedlings were dying with no visible cause
her study of the roots revealed a parasite organism tied to too much watering
she urged watering less often even at the cost of the weakest plants
the growers doubted at first before taking her advice
the death rate among the seedlings dropped by half
she gained the running of an establishment and set up close tracking of every batch
she now passes her experience on to beginners
text: The woman who runs a forest nursery had never meant to do this work. She was studying the chemistry of soils when a disease struck the young trees across her district, and that emergency shaped everything that came after. Seedlings were dying with nothing to show for it, so she took the roots apart and found a fungus that thrived wherever the watering had been too generous. Her advice was hard to swallow: water less often, and accept the loss of the weaker plants. The growers hesitated, then did as she said, and deaths among the seedlings dropped by half. That result won her the running of a nursery, where she brought in a record for every batch, from the seed to the planting out. She trains apprentices now, sure that a tough plant, however small it looks leaving the glasshouse, beats a forward one.

units: the narrator was let down by her first visit to an observation trail
the boards gave nothing but learned names and never said what to look at
a fine stretch of water was hidden behind tall growth and was not signposted
she came back after the trail had been rebuilt
half the boards have been replaced by questions
a gap has been cleared through towards the water
a low seat has been put in to watch the young water insects
the trail now teaches how to spot the marks that animals leave
a shortened route fit for families pushing a pram is still missing
text: Honestly, that nature trail let me down the first time round. The boards lined up learned names and never once told you where to put your eyes, so you walked it the way you walk a corridor. There was a fine pond three steps off the path, hidden behind a screen of reeds, and not a word about it anywhere. I went back after the rebuild, and the difference is plain. Half the boards have gone, replaced by open questions. A gap has been cut through to the water. There is a low bench there now, and from it you watch the larvae flicker under the surface. Fur caught on a bramble, grass pressed flat where something crossed, bark rubbed raw on a trunk: at last you are taught to read the clues yourself. What it still wants is a short loop, no steps and no loose gravel, for families pushing a pram.

units: the writer of the letter writes from her garden to a friend
she compares two cultivated beds she had already spoken of
the bed set high up takes the sun from first light to dusk
the soil of that bed dries out fast and the stems there are short and thick
the flowers of the high bed open early and go over within seven days
the lower bed is sheltered by a wall and sees the sun only from midday
the plants of the lower bed grow taller and flower twice as long
the gap comes mainly from the water in the ground since watering and feeding are identical
a rose moved from the dry bed to the damp one doubled in size in one season
she asks her friend to come before the cold arrives
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the far end of the garden with a notebook on my knees, to tell you about those two beds. The upper one takes sun from first light until it goes: the soil dries out fast, the stems come up short and thick, and the flowers open early only to go over within the week. The lower bed sits against the wall and sees nothing until midday. Everything there grows taller and softer, and the flowering lasts near enough twice as long. The difference is mostly water in the ground, since I water both squares the same and feed them from the same heap. I shifted a rose from the dry bed to the other, and in one season it doubled, throwing out supple shoots I had given up on. Come and see for yourself before the frosts, while the last blooms hold; I shall make tea and bring out two chairs.

units: the renewal of the body covering is put forward as a rebuilding and not a simple discarding
in the snake the old covering comes away in a single piece
the eyes of the snake turn cloudy before that change
the snake rubs against a rough surface to start the tear
in birds the replacement goes piece by piece so that flight is kept
the light fresh plumage grows under the worn one and pushes it off
in insects the young stage breaks down almost wholly to form a winged adult
a damaged covering no longer gives protection
an old covering does not follow an increase in size
a worn plumage keeps out the cold badly
text: What happens when an animal walks out of its own skin? Moulting is no discarded costume, it is a rebuilding. In a snake the old skin peels away whole, in one sleeve: the eyes cloud over first, and then the creature works itself against something rough to start the tear. A bird goes about it feather by feather, so that flight is never lost, and the fresh down comes up beneath the worn plumage and shoulders it off. In an insect the change goes further still, for the grub all but melts away and puts itself together again as a winged adult. And why go to such expense? Because a worn covering stops turning bites, because it cannot follow the growth of the body inside it, and because a shabby coat of feathers holds no warmth. Coming apart, in this trade, is how a creature keeps going.
